This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. A key contribution of this research is the development of a diagnostic tool to detect nonlinearities and justify the adoption of time-varying models for count data. Additionally, an open-access R package, tvparx, has been created to facilitate implementation.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. To address higher values of $k$, we introduce a new algorithm that eliminates the need for poset-related computations, operating with a smaller constant factor. Our experimental results indicate significant performance improvements compared to the previous approach. Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. This work forms the foundation for future research into optimizing policy selection to maximize objective functions and expanding the analysis to more complex multi-task multi-agent problems. The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories. This study examines various mathematical models developed during the current pandemic to tackle key public health concerns regarding epidemic dynamics and their origins. We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, and passage times required to define compartments in these models. Collectively, these examples underscore that a system of differential equations designed for a specific epidemiological challenge relies fundamentally on the epidemiological, medical, and biological context driving its formulation and analysis. Merely fitting differential models to data without considering biological feasibility may yield statistically significant results but will ultimately fail to offer actionable insights for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. Furthermore, utilizing extended datasets does not necessarily enhance the utility of a specific model; for instance, contact information can be integrated into numerous model types without altering their core utility. Consequently, more comprehensive data acquisition will only be beneficial if directed toward appropriate models capable of leveraging it effectively. Finally, we outline several critical considerations for employing models like those discussed herein to guide public health decisions during this pandemic and for future epidemics. The central argument is that detailed data are valuable only when paired with simple, transparent models that clearly communicate the biological and medical assumptions underlying their differential equations, contact graphs, and compartments. Only with such clarity can models serve as effective tools for mitigation, control, and management, and gain the trust necessary to influence public health policy and behavior. We hope this article assists epidemiologists, mathematicians, statisticians, computer scientists, and engineers in recognizing that data volume alone does not ensure success; rather, focusing on the specific epidemiological questions to be answered will drive the development of the most beneficial models for combating the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and addressing future viral threats. While this review has concentrated on differential models applied to mitigation strategies other than lockdowns (as these strategies define the biological boundaries for model creation), similar principles govern the construction and use of models designed to assess lockdown efficacy or evaluate biological and pharmacological interventions. This study reports the potential detection of a nonmonotonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope and surface. KIC 9267654, however, displays a surface rotation rate exceeding that of its bulk envelope, contradicting standard angular momentum conservation expectations. We enhance the spectroscopic constraints on the surface rotation, confirm that pulsation frequencies align with previously determined core and envelope rotation rates, and establish that the star lacks significant chemical peculiarities. Furthermore, we evaluate evidence against the presence of a tidally interacting companion. Finally, we explore possible origins for this anomalous rotation profile, such as the accretion of a giant planet or anomalous angular momentum transport via tidal inertial waves driven by a close substellar companion, and advocate for additional observational and theoretical investigations. The detected rotation profile of low-mass giant star KIC 9267654 may result from angular momentum influx due to the recent loss of a giant planet or inertial waves induced by a close substellar companion. These findings imply either the loss of a planet with an orbital period of approximately 20 hours or the presence of a companion with a period of roughly 0.1 days. Such a configuration represents the closest substellar companion identified around a low-mass giant star to date, offering compelling evidence for the existence of a "Hot Micromasive Planet" in a system where classical Hot Jupiters cannot exist. We propose that similar profiles could arise from low-mass stars in binary systems with companions in ultra-short-period planets or white dwarfs, as well as from single stars possessing a nearby substellar companion and a rotation rate faster than their inertial cutoff. Consequently, one should reconsider the rotational period exclusion criteria used when constraining the properties of low-mass stars, doubles, and remnants in low-mass X-ray binaries, millisecond pulsar binaries, and when selecting targets for the NANOGrav, EPTA, and PPTA pulsar timing arrays. A comprehensive collection of observational constraints on core, envelope/surface, and tidal normal mode pulsations enables the investigation of angular momentum distribution and transport in low- to intermediately-mass stars, provided the surface rotation rate lies below the system's inertial cutoff.

For any rational number $p/q$, numeration in base $p/q$ is defined by a function mapping finite words over the alphabet $A_p=\{0,1,...,p-1\}$ to rational values. The image of this function is denoted by $N_{p/q}$. While $N_{p/q}$ encompasses all nonnegative integers, existing literature typically concentrates on the subset of words evaluating to these integers; this set forms a chaotic, non-context-free language. In contrast, this work examines subsets of $(N_{p/q})^d$ that are $p/q$-recognisable, meaning they can be recognized by finite automata operating over $(A_p)^d$. First, we provide a characterization of these sets as those definable within a specific first-order logic, drawing a parallel to the B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer-based numeration systems. Second, we demonstrate that neither the natural ordering relation nor the modulo-$q$ operator are $p/q$-recognisable. Finally, we offer a positive characterization of finite sets in the form of Diophantine equations over $p/q$ and explore several related findings.

This study tackles the persistent challenge of extracting dynamical information from noisy acoustic emission signals generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant traction velocity. By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics. Additionally, we successfully retrieved the Lyapunov exponent and correlation dimension by optimizing a cost function with a genetic algorithm. Reviving the classic phrase "noise is ordered," this work demonstrates that deterministic chaos manifests in the acoustic emissions of an adhesive tape as the traction velocity varies, due to the stabilization of oscillatory slip via a Hopf bifurcation. To achieve this optimization, we developed an open-source Python package, determinism_noise, available at https://github.com/guptasourav29/determinism_noise, which constitutes a valuable tool for analyzing acoustic emission data. The reported results serve as a validation of the package's effectiveness.

Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, non-sparse, or complex. Extensive comparisons among various iterative methods are conducted both analytically and through extensive numerical simulations. The NN algorithm demonstrates superior performance relative to alternative iterative approaches, as illustrated by a significant performance boost in "real-time" metrics for NN-based mMIMO access points when handling large matrices. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the optimal NN order (and corresponding inception depth) to maximize convergence speed. Notably, an "infinity-order" NN method (using high orders up to a practical limit) is formulated to minimize convergence time (or maximize real-time performance) for specific matrix sizes, particularly when NN is implemented in parallel. Finally, we extend the NN approach to adaptively track changes in large matrices without requiring restarts; this "Nested-Neumann" (N2) variant outperforms both NI and N1 methods. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. The rise of outsourced training and machine learning as a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice.

This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. An implementation within a Federated Learning context is included for comparison. Additionally, we conduct an initial exploration of how a prior over data distributions at each node influences learning performance. The code for our methods is available at https://github.com/jialin111777/RW-Learning-and-FL. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in model size alongside significant accuracy gains across various video recognition datasets. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed hardware accelerator TIE, our FDHT-LSTM architecture achieves higher throughput, better area efficiency, and improved energy efficiency on the LSTM-Youtube workload. Similarly, on the LSTM-UCF workload, our design outperforms TIE in throughput and energy efficiency while maintaining comparable area efficiency. Sources for the FDHT-LSTM model and the corresponding hardware accelerator are available at https://github.com/Stevedu/FDHT_LSTM_Model_and_Hardware_Accelerator.

This paper examines the Schrödinger equation featuring a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity in the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^{d}$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the presence of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising in the second derivative of the variance that carry an unfavorable sign. To address this, our primary approach involves introducing a novel modified variance that is bounded from below and strictly concave for the specific solutions under consideration. Notably, this method does not require the solutions to be radially symmetric. Our results indicate that boundary effects can be overcame by the focusing nonlinearity when in the supercritical regime. Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Discourse markers, such as {\it by contrast} and {\it happily}, are words or phrases that indicate semantic and/or pragmatic connections between clauses or sentences. Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Using DiscSense, we present a bottom-up analysis of the connection between discourse markers and semantic relations in Discourse Grammars. Our findings indicate that a single marker can contradict another with respect to specific discourse relation categories. Furthermore, we provide a first automatic classification of professional discourse markers into relation categories based on their frequency of co-occurrence with discourse relation categories, excluding categories with insufficient evidence. We conclude by outlining potential applications of this work and proposing directions for future research. The datasets introduced in this study are available at https://github.com/discourse-representational-theory/DiscSense and will be publicly released soon.

This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. Finally, we derive a lower bound for the lightest neutral meson's mass based on the coherence of its neutral current interactions.
